html:
In about 1431, by tradition, armies of Ayutthaya sacked Angkor, and the Khmer kings soon left it for the area of Phnom Penh in the south. It marks the end of the Khmer Empire of Angkor.

The decline had deeper causes: the wars with Siam, the spread of Theravada Buddhism, which needed no great god-king temples, failing water works after droughts and floods, and a shift of trade to the sea.

Later kings ruled from Longvek, Oudong and Phnom Penh, often squeezed between Siam and Vietnam. Angkor Wat itself was never abandoned by monks, but the city was overgrown until French explorers publicised it in the 1860s. See Ayutthaya.
